title: Known in the breaking of bread (Luke 24:13–35)
hookLine: two disciples, seven miles, burning hearts, and bread broken at dusk

cards: The same Sunday, late afternoon. Two of Jesus's followers are walking out of Jerusalem toward a village called Emmaus, about seven miles away. One is named Cleopas; the other Luke never names.
They're going over it and over it, the way people do after a funeral. A stranger catches up and asks what they're talking about. They stop, faces sad.

Are you the only visitor in Jerusalem who doesn't know what happened? And they tell him, ending in the past tense, in the King James words: "But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel."

teach.h: WE TRUSTED: HOPE IN THE PAST TENSE.
teach.b: We trusted. Past. Their hope is something that used to be.
They even mention the women's report about the empty tomb, and it hasn't helped. Luke tells us their eyes were holden, kept from recognizing him.

Then the stranger begins with Moses and all the prophets and walks them through everything in the scriptures about himself, seven miles of it. At the village it's getting dark, and he acts as if he's going on.
They press him: "Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent." That plea later gave a hymn its title, Abide with Me. So he stays.
At the table, the guest does the host's job: he takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them, the same four movements as the feeding of the five thousand, and the last supper.
"And their eyes were opened, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight." And then, looking at each other: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?"
They go back to Jerusalem that same hour, and tell how he was known of them in breaking of bread.
Some Christians hear this story as the shape of their Sunday worship: the scriptures opened, then the bread broken.
He wasn't recognized in the explaining.

teach.h: KNOWN OF THEM IN BREAKING OF BREAD.
teach.b: He was recognized at the table.

how: Some churches describe their Sunday worship in the shape of the Emmaus story: first the scriptures read and explained, then bread broken at the Lord's table.

games.q: you've walked seven miles with a stranger who opened the scriptures to you. you've reached home, it's getting dark, and he's going on. what do you do?
o: press him to stay and eat with you.
games.why: "abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent." he stays, breaks the bread, and they know him.

practice: Think of someone who's been walking with you lately, maybe without you really noticing: a neighbor, a new coworker, a friend who's been quiet.

Picture the moment they'd usually head home, and you saying, stay, it's getting late, eat with us, and breaking ordinary bread together. If you pray, you can ask to recognize God in the people at your table.

wordCard.voice: Cleopas. One of the two disciples walking to Emmaus who didn't recognize the risen Jesus until he broke the bread at their table.

orig.note: Greek: the breaking of the bread. Luke uses the same phrase in Acts for the first Christians' shared meals.
